codex_rationale: D1 decides what text from an untrusted note reaches the answer model. Codex has now overturned three of this package line's declared limitations and found two classes Agent C had passed. The high-risk criteria are met.

design.change: classify_markup runs the pass; if an opener turns out never to close, it records that opener as ordinary text and runs the pass AGAIN with it. Each restart settles one opener, so it terminates, and the classification finally returned was computed with the right answer from the first line - fence state included.
design.why_this_closes_the_class: the give-back could only undo TEXT. State - fence tracking above all - had already been computed from the wrong premise. Deciding before acting means there is no wrong premise to undo.
design.one_state_machine: the restart re-runs the same pass rather than adding a second traversal, so the two cannot drift apart
design.termination: bounded by len(lines) + 1 passes. Each restart settles one opener and a note has at most that many, so the bound is never reached while this function is correct. It is a bound rather than a progress check because a progress check only catches the shape of non-progress it tests for - which is exactly how the previous wording came to be false.

blocking.summary: The restart is O(N^2) and build_index applies no file-size cap, so note CONTENT can delay an index rebuild for hours. Codex classes this as an index-build denial-of-service surface.
blocking.measured: 2000 unterminated openers: base 0.002s, candidate 1.566s. 1000: base 0.001s, candidate 0.392s. The predecessor was linear.
blocking.why_declaring_it_was_not_enough: this receipt declared the quadratic as a known limitation. Codex has now made the same call three times - that a declared limitation is honest about implementation scope and dishonest about acceptance impact - and been upheld each time. A regression that hands note content control over indexing time is not a footnote.

blocking.summary: _RULE_LINE_RE is r"^[ \t]*[-=_*]{3,}[ \t]*$", which accepts any MIXTURE of those characters. A Markdown thematic break is three or more of ONE marker (*** --- ___), and '===' is a setext underline rather than a break at all.
blocking.reproduced: a standalone line '-=_*' is kept by the base and deleted by this candidate
blocking.why_it_matters: this is a cleanup destruction path, not missing coverage. The receipt declared setext flattening but not the wider deletion of mixed-punctuation lines.

what_is_settled: the give-back is gone and the state-restoration class with it - Codex accepts the restart design as correct

root_cause_of_each.P1: the restart re-scans from line 1 every time. It does not need to: state flows strictly forward and literal_openers only affects lines at or after the settled opener, so everything before it is identical on every pass.
root_cause_of_each.P2: the rule pattern was written as a character class when a thematic break is a repeated single marker. The character class was inherited from the base, where it never fired because the pattern was inert - so this package made a latent error operative.

recommended_next.description: Fix both. P2 is one regex: ^[ \t]*(\*{3,}|-{3,}|_{3,})[ \t]*$, dropping '=' from the break markers and requiring a single repeated marker; setext underlines then need their own decision. P1 is resuming the restart from the settled opener rather than rescanning - keep the classified prefix and the fence state as they stood just before that line and continue, which makes it linear. Both are well understood, neither is speculative, and this is the first stop in this defect's history where the fix direction is not in doubt.

Cap the note size in build_index and merge with P2 fixed only. That removes the denial-of-service surface without making the algorithm linear, at the price of silently skipping very large notes - which is its own product decision.

escalation.executor_note: Eleven attempts across five packages. What is different this time: Codex accepts the mechanism, both remaining findings are small and fully diagnosed, and neither is about the part that has been failing repeatedly. I would take option A.
